title.en: The Magic Ring: Carlos and the Goddess of the Sea
title.zh: 魔戒：卡洛斯與海之女神

region.en: Jaro, Iloilo, central Philippines (story very popular among the Visayans)
region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省哈羅（故事甚為流行）

texts.period: Visayan oral tale ('Ang Singsing nga Tantanang'); collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring (Ang Singsing nga Tantanan)', eBook #8299

summary.en: Ashamed to beg, Carlos stands beneath the princess's window and is spat upon; his retort — that the Goddess of the Sea, star on forehead and moon on throat, would not dare — costs him his head unless she appears within a week. An eagle and the king of the fishes carry him to her golden house; she gives him her diamond ring — touch it thrice for her help, six times and she appears. When the whole court waits for the goddess, Carlos touches the ring six times and is saved; he marries Florentina, builds a chapel of gold, and his mother dies of happiness — though he never learns the meaning of his name.
summary.zh: 恥於行乞的卡洛斯立於公主窗下，竟被唾面；他反唇譏她不及『額有星、喉有月的海之女神』，遂以性命為注：一週內請不來女神便處絞。鷹王與魚王引他至女神金宮；女神贈鑽戒——叩三下得助，叩六下現身。滿朝引頸等待之時，卡洛斯六叩金戒，女神降臨，全場震懾。他娶得佛洛倫蒂娜，以黃金造禮拜堂，老母含笑而逝——唯其名字之義，至死未明。

sensitivity.note: Visayan folktale recorded by Fansler from a Gonzaga narrator (Jaro, Iloilo); archival record. Fansler knows no variants; the helpful animals lack the usual motivation.

passages.text: In the town of X, not far from the kingdom of Don Fernando, there lived an old religious woman named Carmen, who had a son named Carlos; she had been a widow since Carlos was nine months old, and was poor, poor even to raggedness. 'I have named you Carlos because I love you. For me, no name is prettier than yours. Every letter in it means something' — but when Carlos asked her to tell him the meaning of his name she said, 'I'll tell it to you later. First go to the king's palace, and there beg something for us to eat. O my son! If you only knew the miseries I have had to endure to bring you up, you would not refuse this request of your poor mother.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Carlos pitied his mother very much, so he ran towards the king's palace to beg some food; but when he reached the gate he hesitated to enter, for he was ashamed to beg, and went and stood silently under the orange-tree which was not far from the princess's window. As Carlos was looking at the declining sun with tears in his eyes, the princess raised her window and unintentionally spit on his head. Carlos's eyes flashed; he looked at the princess sternly and said, 'If the Goddess of the Sea, who has a star on her forehead and a moon on her throat, does not dare to spit on me, how can you — you who are but the shadow of her power and beauty?' At these harsh words the princess fainted; when she came to herself she cried, and her father, hearing her story, instantly ordered Carlos to be seized and brought into his presence. 'If within a week you cannot show me that what you said to my daughter is true, you'll be hanged without mercy.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.

passages.text: With tears in his eyes and his thoughts devoted to God, Carlos walked down the shore of the Golden River and sat down to rest under a pagatpat-tree; an eagle which had a nest at the very top of the tree saw him crying and pitied him very much: 'Come, Carlos, come! And I'll lead you to the right path.' At the mouth of the river she shouted, 'O king of the fishes! Come and help me, for I am in great need of assistance'; the king of the fishes appeared, and, as the fish could not refuse the request of the queen of the birds, he said to Carlos, 'Carlos, lie on my back and close your eyes: within five minutes you'll be in the home of the goddess.' When he opened his eyes, he found himself in a very beautiful house, lying on a golden bed, and beside him was standing a beautiful woman with a star on her forehead and a moon on her throat. Carlos related his story, and the goddess could not refuse help to one who had spoken so well of her beauty: she took her diamond ring off her finger and gave it to Carlos, saying, 'Take this ring with you. Whenever you want or need my help, touch the ring thrice, and say, O God, help me! If the king wants my presence, touch the ring six times, and I'll appear before you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When morning came the next day, Carlos was ordered into the king's presence, all the lords and nobles of the kingdom being in the palace, anxious to see the Goddess of the Sea. It was already eight o'clock, and the goddess had not yet appeared. 'Where is she, Carlos?' 'She cannot come; but, if your Highness wants me to, I'll give you a trunk filled with gold in exchange for my life.' 'No. What we want is the Goddess of the Sea. If you cannot show her to us, prepare to be hanged.' Carlos touched the ring six times, and the beautiful Goddess of the Sea appeared; all were amazed to see a woman with curly hair, a star on her forehead, a moon on her throat, and wearing a white dress glistening with diamonds. 'Carlos is an enchanter!' cried the king, and he ran to embrace the goddess; in five minutes she disappeared, and Carlos's life was saved. Don Fernando now proposed to marry his daughter Florentina to Carlos; at first the princess hesitated to say yes, but at last she consented, and Carlos was glad to marry the beautiful princess — but before the marriage took place, he went to get his poor mother, who was anxiously awaiting his return home. Carlos with his diamond ring could now have everything he needed; in fact, he made the chapel in which he was married all of gold, and the wedding-dress of the princess was adorned with diamonds. Immediately after the wedding, poor Carmen died of happiness. Carlos continued to live in the palace with his wife Florentina, but he never came to know the meaning of his name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 44 'The Magic Ring'; not verbatim.

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45a 'Maria and the Golden Slipper', eBook #8299

summary.en: Servant-girl Maria is told by a crab — her dead mother — to bury its shell, from which grows a wish-tree that clothes her for Prince Malecadel's balls in a coach of fine horses and golden slippers. Fleeing at midnight she loses one slipper; the prince's order — 'The lady whom this slipper fits is to be my wife' — finds her foot exactly, the other slipper beneath her dress, and her sisters faint with astonishment as she becomes the prince's wife, dear to them from that day on.
summary.zh: 侍女瑪利亞聽從螃蟹——她亡母所化——之囑，將蟹殼埋於園中；長出的神樹為她變出華服、駿馬之車與一雙金鞋，赴王子馬里克阿德爾的舞會。午夜逃歸失落一鞋；王子懸令『鞋合腳者為妻』——瑪利亞穿上正合，裙下另鞋一出，兩位姊姊驚得幾近昏厥。她成為王子之妻，從此亦得家人珍愛。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog Cinderella tale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Fansler notes Crab-as-mother and the shell-tree; cf. the Visayan Abadeja variant and Rusk's 'The Wonderful Tree' (mother drowned, fins planted).

passages.text: Once there lived a couple who had an only daughter, Maria. When Maria was a little girl her mother died; a few years later Maria's father fell in love with a widow named Juana, who had two daughters, the elder Rosa and the younger Damiana, and when Maria was grown to be a young woman her father married the woman Juana. Maria continued to live with her father and step-mother, but Juana and her two daughters treated Maria as a servant: she had to do all the work in the house — cook the food, wash the clothes, clean the floors — and the only clothes she herself had to wear were ragged and dirty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Prince Malecadel wanted to get married, so he gave a ball to which he invited all the ladies in his kingdom, saying that the most beautiful of all was to be his wife. When Damiana and Rosa knew that all the ladies were invited, they began to discuss what clothes they would wear to the ball; but poor Maria was in the river, washing the clothes, very sad and weeping, for she had no clothes at all in which she could appear at the prince's fête. While she was washing, a crab approached her, and said, 'Why are you crying, Maria? Tell me the reason, for I am your mother.' While she was talking to the crab, Juana came up, very angry, and ordered her to catch the crab and cook it for their dinner; Maria seized the crab and carried it to the house, at first refusing to cook it, for she knew that it was her mother — but Juana whipped her so hard that at last she was forced to obey. Before it was put in the earthen pot to be cooked, the crab said to Maria, 'Maria, don't eat my flesh, but collect all my shell after I am eaten, and bury the pieces in the garden near the house. They will grow into a tree, and you can have what you want if you will only ask the tree for it.' After her parents had eaten the flesh of the crab, Maria collected all its shell and buried it in the garden; at twilight she saw a tree standing on the very spot where she had buried the shell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When night came, Rosa and Damiana went to the ball, and Juana retired for the night as soon as her daughters were gone; when Maria saw that her aunt was sleeping, she went into the garden and asked the tree for what she wanted. The tree changed her clothes into very beautiful ones, and furnished her with a fine coach drawn by four fine horses, and a pair of golden slippers. 'You must be in your house before twelve o'clock. If you are not, your clothes will be changed into ragged, dirty ones again, and your coach will disappear.' At the ball she was received by the prince very graciously: she was the most beautiful of all, and sat between her two sisters, neither of whom recognized her; the prince danced with her all the time. When Maria saw that it was half-past eleven, she bade farewell to the prince and went home, where the tree changed her beautiful clothes back into her old ones and the coach disappeared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next night the prince gave another ball; Maria again went to the garden to ask for beautiful clothes, and this time was given a coach drawn by five horses, the tree again warning her to return before twelve. The prince was delighted to see her, and danced with her the whole evening — but Maria was so enchanted that she forgot to notice the time; while she was dancing she heard the clock striking twelve, and ran as fast as she could down stairs and out the palace-door, in her haste dropping one of her golden slippers. One of her golden slippers she had with her; but the other, which she had dropped at the door, was found by one of the guards, who gave it to the prince, saying that the slipper had been lost by the beautiful lady who ran out of the palace when the clock was striking twelve. 'The lady whom this slipper fits is to be my wife,' said the prince to all the people present. The first house visited was the one in which Maria lived: Rosa tried to put the slipper on her foot, but her foot was much too big; then Damiana put it on her foot, but her foot was too small — the two sisters tried and tried again to make the slipper fit, but in vain. Then Maria told them she would try; but her sisters said, 'Your feet are very dirty. This golden slipper will not go on your foot, for your feet are larger than ours,' and laughed at her — but the guard who had brought the slipper said, 'Let her try. It is the prince's order that all shall try.' Then Maria put it on, and it fitted her foot exactly; she then drew the other slipper from underneath her dress and put it on her other foot, and when the two sisters saw the two slippers on Maria's feet, they almost fainted with astonishment. So Maria became the wife of the prince, and from that time on she was very dear to her sisters and aunt.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Maria and the Golden Slipper'; not verbatim.

title.en: Abadeja: The Black Handkerchief Made White
title.zh: 阿巴德婭：白帕染黑、黑帕洗白

region.zh: 菲律賓萊特省拜拜（米沙鄢故事）

texts.period: Visayan oral tale from Leyte; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45b 'Abadeja', eBook #8299

summary.en: Orphaned Abadeja, abused by her step-mother, is set impossible tasks — a white handkerchief black, a black one white; a torn mat made new — each solved by a beautiful woman of the high trees. A gift chicken killed and cooked leaves only its feet, which the woman tells her to plant east and west in a forest garden, where they grow into air, bearing pearls, diamonds, gold dresses, rings, bracelets, shoes, necklaces, and ear-rings. The rich man's son who steals a ring can only be cured by the girl whose hand removes it — Abadeja in a gold dress — and she becomes his wife, the beautiful woman attending the wedding unseen.
summary.zh: 繼母苛待孤女阿巴德婭，屢出難題——白帕染黑、黑帕洗白、破蓆復新——皆由高樹間的美婦化解。受贈的雞被殺烹，只餘雙足；美婦教她把左右足分植東西，森林小園中竟長出珠寶、金衣、戒指、手鐲與項鍊。富家公子摘戒指中毒腫，唯有取戒者可為其妻——金衣加身的阿巴德婭一觸即解。二人成婚，美婦隱身觀禮。

sensitivity.note: Visayan Cinderella variant from Leyte (narrator unrecorded), printed by Fansler; archival record. Fansler notes its distinctive items: the black-white handkerchief task, the tree from chicken-feet, and the ring-cure marriage device.

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived in the town of Baybay a man whose name was Abac; the name of his wife was Abadesa, and they had a beautiful daughter named Abadeja. The mother died when her daughter was about thirteen years old, and in a year her father married again, a widow who had three daughters. The second wife envied her step-daughter because Abadeja was much more beautiful than her own children: consequently she treated the poor girl very badly, made her do all the hard work, and punished her severely when she could not do the work.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One evening the step-mother said to Abadeja, 'Take these two handkerchiefs to the river and wash them. The white one must be black, and the black one white, when you bring them back to me. If they are not, I shall beat you.' Abadeja went to the river, where she sat down on a rock and began to cry — until a beautiful woman stood before her, took the handkerchiefs, and in an instant they were transformed; then she gave them back to Abadeja and invited the girl to come see her any time she needed help. The next morning Abadeja was ordered to put some rice on a mat in the sun to dry; while she was in the house doing other work, a pig came, ate up the rice, and tore the mat to pieces — and her step-mother whipped her severely for having lost the rice and told her she would have to repair the mat so that it was as good as new. Abadeja took the mat and went across the river, crying; the beautiful woman met her again, and, taking her by the hand, led her to her home among the high trees, where she took the mat from the girl and waved it in the air — immediately it became a whole mat again. Then she gave Abadeja a beautifully-colored chicken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next day, when Abadeja was away from the house, her cruel step-mother took the chicken, killed it, and cooked it; when the girl returned, only the feet of her chicken were left. She cried over her loss, and ran to the river to ask the beautiful woman what she should do — and the beautiful woman told the girl to take the chicken's feet and plant them in the forest. Abadeja went home, took the feet, and carried them with her to the forest; there she made a little garden, in which she planted the right foot toward the east, and the left foot toward the west. A month later she visited her garden in the woods, and was astonished to see that the feet had grown up into the air, and that they bore pearls, diamonds, gold dresses, rings, bracelets, shoes, necklaces, and ear-rings. She was delighted, but she did not tell her step-mother about her garden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the son of the richest man in Baybay came across this little garden in the forest, picked off a ring, and put it on his finger; when he reached home, his finger began to swell. His father called in all the best physicians, but they could not remove the ring; then he called in all the girls of the town, and said that the one who could take the ring from the finger of his son should be his son's wife. All the girls of the town tried except Abadeja, who did not try because her mother would not allow her to go — at last someone told the rich man that there was still a girl who had not tried, and that it was Abadeja, so he sent for her. Now her step-mother did not dare refuse to let her go; Abadeja ran to her little garden, put on one of the gold dresses, and went to the rich man's house — and as soon as she touched the ring, it slid off. The next day Abadeja was married to the son of the rich man; the beautiful woman attended the wedding unseen by everyone except Abadeja, and the young couple lived happily for many years.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 45 'Abadeja'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Poor: Doña Maria on Her Mountain
title.zh: 窮漢胡安與山上的瑪利亞

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog folk-tale form of the romance 'King Asuero'; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor', eBook #8299

summary.en: A sad king proclaims half his kingdom to whoever fetches Doña Maria from her distant mountain. Beggar Juan shares his alms with an old woman who equips him: a handkerchief that produces whatever is asked, the lean last horse that can endure hardships, an ant's leg and eagle's feathers whose ashes summon armies of helpers. The saddled horse lures Doña Maria from her garden; the king, in love with her, sets Juan a death-task — separate a hundred cavans of mixed rice and transport her palace in one night — and the ants and birds of Juan's kindness perform both by morning.
summary.zh: 鬱鬱的國王懸賞半國，求人自遠山請來瑪利亞。行乞的胡安與老嫗分享所得，得手帕、瘦馬、蟻足與鷹羽。備鞍的駿馬誘瑪利亞出園；垂涎的國王刁難胡安：一夜之內分揀百石糙米、並將山中宮殿搬來——胡安焚蟻足與鷹羽，萬蟻分米、群鳥搬殿，拂曉功成，遂與瑪利亞成婚。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from a Zafra narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Clearly derived from the Tagalog metrical romance 'The Life of King Asuero, Doña Maria, and Juan the Poor in the City of Jerusalem,' but told as a folk-tale; Fansler includes it for completeness of Philippine popular literature.

passages.text: Many years ago there lived a king who was always sad; he used to go to a mountain and climb the highest tree that was growing there. One day, when he was in the top of the tree, he saw on another high mountain a beautiful princess, Doña Maria; when he returned home to his palace, he sent a proclamation all over his kingdom, saying that the one who could take Doña Maria from her mountain and bring her before him should have one-half of his kingdom. Juan was a beggar; and it was his custom, whenever he saw a beggar like himself, to share with that beggar the alms which had been given him. One day he saw a wretched old woman, and out of pity for her he gave her all the food he had begged that day; then the old woman, who knew of the proclamation of the king, said to Juan, 'You must tell the king, my boy, that you will fetch Doña Maria for him' — and at last she persuaded Juan to go by telling him that she would accompany him, and promising her help.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After Juan had visited the palace and told the king that he would bring the princess Doña Maria to him, the poor boy and the old woman set out on their journey to the distant mountain; when they reached the gates of the city, the old woman said to Juan, 'Juan, I am very tired, and I cannot go any farther, but I will give you this handkerchief. When you come to the first mountain, you must spread the handkerchief on the ground, and many fat horses will approach you; but I advise you not to choose any of them. You must choose the very last one, which will be lean and weak-looking. That is the horse which can endure hardships, and which will be able to carry you to the princess's palace.' Juan followed the advice of the old woman, and mounted the thin horse.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When he had ridden very far, he saw before him a hill full of ants, and was afraid to pass over lest the ants should devour him and his animal. 'You must ask the handkerchief for food, and we will feed the ants,' said the horse. Juan spread out the handkerchief and asked it to bring him much food; after he had scattered it on the ground for the ants, the leader of the ants approached Juan and said, 'Since you have been very kind to us, I will give you one of my legs; and at any time you want aid from us, you must burn the leg, and let the ashes be carried by the wind. Then we will come to help you.' Again, when the sky was full of birds flying around and looking for food, Juan fed them all they wanted to eat, and the king of the birds, the eagle, flew up to him: 'To repay you for your kindness, I will give you some feathers from my wings. Any time you want aid from us, just burn some of the feathers, and let the ashes be carried by the wind. Then we will come to you.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When they came near the palace of Doña Maria, the horse told Juan to hide, and said that he alone would enter her garden; but before he should hide, Juan should ask his handkerchief for a complete equipment of saddle and bridle, so that the horse could be mounted by a lady. When the princess saw the horse she became very angry, 'Who is the one who is so bold as to let his horse enter my garden?' — but she could see no one, so she said to herself, 'I will mount this horse and find out who its owner is'; she mounted the horse, which immediately ran to the place where Juan was hiding and told him to get up on its back, carrying them swiftly back to the small house of Juan. The king, accompanied by all his retinue, went in great state to Juan's house, made over to him one-half of his dominion, and took Doña Maria back to his palace — but Doña Maria was very beautiful, and the king fell deeply in love with her. 'Only the one who can do what I wish him to do shall be my husband. I will mix one hundred cavans of husked rice with one hundred cavans of unhusked rice. He who in one night can separate the two kinds of rice, and also bring my palace here to your kingdom, shall be married to me,' she said — and told the king there was one who could accomplish the tasks, and that was Juan. 'To-night you must separate the grain into two piles, and also transport the palace of Doña Maria to my kingdom. If you have not done both by to-morrow morning, you shall lose your head.' Juan went away very sad toward the mountain; as he was walking along, he met the thin horse which had helped him before: 'Don't be sad, Juan! You can accomplish both those difficult tasks. Don't you remember the leg of the ant and the feathers of the eagle which were given to you, and the promise of the ant and eagle?' So Juan took the ant's leg and the feathers from his pocket, burned them, and threw the ashes into the air; in a short time thousands of birds and ants came to him and asked him what he wanted — 'I want the palace of Doña Maria brought here before daybreak, and the two hundred cavans of mixed rice separated.' The birds flew to the mountain to get the palace, and the ants hastened to the king's grounds to separate the unhusked from the husked rice; by morning both tasks were completed, so Juan was married to Doña Maria, for she would have no other husband.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 46 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Fate of an Envious Woman

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman', eBook #8299

summary.en: Pockmarked Maria, forsaken by her husband Juan for the beautiful Flora, prays before the image of St. Vicente Ferrer, whose animated hand touches her face into extraordinary beauty; Juan returns to the wife he had despised. Envious Flora kneels at the same image — and becomes as black and ugly as the mistress of a Kaffir household, her lips thick and coarse, her nose as long as a monkey's tail; she pines away and dies, while Juan confesses his sins and the two live in peace and happiness.
summary.zh: 麻面的瑪利亞被丈夫胡安拋棄；她在聖維森特·費雷爾像前祈禱，聖像之手撫面，醜女化為絕色，浪子重歸髮妻。妒火中燒的弗洛拉同往聖像前祈求——竟變得如卡菲爾家的黑婦，唇厚鼻長如猿尾。她羞慚而歸，憔悴而死；胡安懺悔贖罪，夫妻自此安樂終老。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog tale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (Batangas); archival record. Toads-and-Diamonds group with two wives instead of two sisters; Fansler compares the Visayan 'The Two Wives and the Witch' and Lal Behari Day's Bengal tale No. 22. The period's colonial comparisons are retained as recorded and noted.

passages.text: There lived once upon a time a young couple of the middle class: the man was a reckless scapegrace and spendthrift, but the woman was a pious, faithful, and virtuous housewife — Juan the husband, Maria the wife. One of the worst things about Juan was that he spent on another woman the greater part of the money which Maria could with difficulty scrape together; this other woman's name was Flora, who surpassed Maria in personal charm but in real worth was greatly Maria's inferior. Hence Maria soon grew distasteful to her husband, and after a year of married life he sought to be entertained by a more beautiful woman, spending most of his time in listless indolence by the side of Flora, returning home only to get his meals, which Maria prepared with the greatest care. But her efforts were all to no purpose: in vain did Maria array herself in her best clothes, and scent herself with the most delicate perfumes — her face remained pitted with small-pox scars, as before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Years came and passed, and Juan became more and more harsh to his wife. At last Maria sought the aid of St. Vicente Ferrer: she knelt before the image, and asked the saint to rescue her husband from the pit into which he had fallen. Her prayers were soon answered: the image became animated; it touched her face several times, and in a few seconds Maria was converted into an extraordinary beauty — her once rough skin was now smooth and velvety. She then went to the window to await her husband's return; when he arrived an hour later, he was at first unwilling to come up into the house, for he did not believe that the beautiful woman was his wife, but at last she disclosed her true self to him. A great change now came over Juan: the once despised wife now began to enjoy the caresses of her husband, who pressed her close to his heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Days elapsed, and Flora began to get uneasy at her home, wondering why Juan did not come to see her; at length she went to his house, and after asking Maria how she had acquired her beauty decided to try her fortune also. She too knelt before the image of St. Vicente Ferrer — but, alas! instead of becoming as white and as beautiful as she hoped, she became black and ugly; her once delicate lips became thick and coarse, and her nose became as long as a monkey's tail. Filled with shame at her appearance, and with a consciousness of her own guilt, she went home, where she pined away and died. The once homely Maria, whose home had rung with the taunt and ridicule of those who made fun of her ugliness, now graced her house with sweet smiles and engaging features, which drew scores of visitors to her home; Juan confessed his sins and underwent penance for his wickedness, and the two lived together in peace and happiness the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 47 'The Fate of an Envious Woman'; not verbatim.
